1.title: Clockwork Beneath the Floorboards
1.html:
The pendulum did not belong in the pantry. It hung from a meat hook, dripping something thick and dark onto the salted floorboards, tick-tock, tick-tock, setting a frantic tempo that Arthur felt in his teeth.

He knelt, ignoring the smear on his knees, and traced the groove worn into the oak. The house was barely forty years old, yet this channel looked ancient, carved by centuries of heavy chains dragging across the grain. Above him, the floorboards of the master bedroom groaned under the weight of Inspector Vance's heavy boots.

"Find anything down there, Arthur?" Vance called out, his voice muffled by the lath and plaster. "Or are you just making friends with the mice?"

"The foundation isn't stone," Arthur said, his voice tight. He scraped a fingernail along the baseboard, dislodging a wedge of gray mortar. "It's hollow."

A low thud signaled Vance’s descent down the narrow back stairs. The Inspector squeezed into the cramped pantry, his trench coat smelling of damp wool and autumn rain. He looked at the swinging pendulum, then down at Arthur. Tick-tock.

"Lord Harrington swore there was nothing beneath the ground floor," Vance muttered, pulling a brass-trimmed flashlight from his pocket. "Said this was built on virgin soil after the Great Fire.

"Lord Harrington lies about the price of his port, why not his dirt?" Arthur stood up, wiping his hands on a rag. He pointed at the gap in the baseboard. "Shine it in there.

Vance clicked the light on and dropped to one knee, angling the beam into the dark recess. The light caught the dull gleam of polished brass, rusted iron, and something pale and white that did not reflect the light the way metal did.

"Good God," Vance breathed.

It was not a cellar. It was a mechanism. A colossal array of interlocking brass cogs, weighted levers, and massive drums spanned the entire footprint of the manor. Hanging from the ceiling beams of this subterranean vault were dozens of swinging pendulums, synchronized in a macabre, deafening chorus that vibrated through the foundation walls.

And woven into the iron spokes of the central drive wheel were scraps of expensive wool fabric, silver buttons, and fragments of bone.

"The town records," Arthur whispered, watching a heavy iron piston rise and crush a dried rose caught in its teeth. "The disappearance reports from the last three decades. They didn't vanish into the moors, Inspector."

Vance stood slowly, his face drained of color in the harsh LED glow. He stared at the pantry ceiling—directly up toward the master bedroom where Lord Harrington was currently waiting with his solicitor.

"The house isn't built on a foundation," Vance said, the horror dawning in his eyes as the steady, relentless rhythm echoed around them. "It's built on a clock."

Tick-tock.

2.title: Unspooled Thread and Tea
2.html:
The fifth time Maya knocked the half-empty ceramic mug off the drafting table, Julian didn't sigh. He simply reached out, his calloused palm catching it a fraction of an inch above the linoleum floor before the dark roast could stain her new linen trousers.

"That's three mugs, two sketchbooks, and a half-eaten brioche today, Red," he murmured, setting the cup safely back onto its cork coaster. His knuckles brushed her wrist as he pulled his hand away—a fleeting, accidental friction that sent a familiar, low-voltage current straight up her forearm.

Maya didn't pull back. Instead, she let out a breathless laugh, leaning her forehead against his shoulder. The tweed of his jacket smelled like cedarwood, damp autumn air, and the faint, sweet trace of pipe tobacco he’d abandoned years ago. "My brain is refusing to translate the floor plans into three dimensions. I think my spatial awareness has packed its bags and moved to Portugal."

"It hasn't moved. It's just exhausted." Julian’s hand moved up, his thumb rhythmically tracing the tense knot at the nape of her neck. The warmth of his touch was an anchor in the chaotic storm of paper and deadlines. "You've been hunched over this table since four this morning. The client doesn't need the final render until Tuesday."

"The client is my mother's notoriously difficult brother-in-law, which means he expects the Sistine Chapel drafted in pastel blue by tomorrow noon." Maya closed her eyes, melting into the steady, reliable rhythm of Julian’s breathing.

They had been business partners for four years, navigating zoning laws, difficult contractors, and the agonizing process of building an architecture firm from the ground up. Somewhere around the second year, the boundaries had begun to blur. Late nights ordering cold pizza morphed into shared playlists and arguments over who made better espresso. Yet, the unspoken truth hung between them like a load-bearing pillar neither dared to inspect too closely.

Julian tilted her chin up with a gentle finger. His dark eyes were impossibly soft, stripped of the professional polish he wore for clients. "Leave it."

"I can't."

"You can." He leaned in, his voice dropping an octave, slipping past her defenses with the ease of long practice. "The lines will still be here tomorrow. But you won't be, if you keep running on adrenaline and caffeine."

He reached past her, the heat of his chest pressing against her back as he deftly capped her drafting pen and laid it to rest in the wooden tray. The finality of the gesture sent a shiver down her spine. He didn't step away. Instead, his arms wrapped around her waist, pulling her flush against him. Maya let out a soft sigh, her hands finding their way to the lapels of his jacket, gripping the fabric as if she were anchoring herself to the only real thing in the room.

"You're dangerously persuasive, Julian Vance," she whispered against his collarbone.

"Only when it matters." He pressed a tender, lingering kiss to her temple, his lips lingering against her skin. "Come on. Let's go make some actual tea, and you can tell me all about how much you hate your uncle's taste in crown molding."

Maya smiled, finally letting the pencil slip from her fingers entirely. As he led her away from the drafting table, hand intertwined with hers, she realized she wouldn't mind being lost in this particular blueprint for the rest of her life.

3.title: The Glass Bridge
3.html:
The marrow-chill of the North scraped against Kaelen’s collarbones as the third link snapped. Below them, three thousand feet of grey mist churned like greasy wool, swallowing the sound of falling iron.

"Don't look down," Vesper breathed. Her knuckles were the colour of old lard where she gripped the remaining guy-wire.

Kaelen didn't answer. His tongue felt like a dried salted mackerel against the roof of his mouth. He shifted his weight, testing the stability of the frosted basalt slab beneath his right boot. It groaned—a high, singing vibration that travelled straight up his shins and settled behind his teeth. The bridge wasn't built for men; it was strung together by the First Cartographers using dragon-sinew and slag-glass, a translucent spine spanning the Great Tear. Every decade, the magic drained a little more, leaving the path more ghost than stone.

From the southern pylon, something scraped against the ice.

It wasn't the wind. The wind wailed a steady, hollow alto. This was a wet, rhythmic schalc-schalc, the sound of heavy scales dragging over frozen ruts.

A shape detached itself from the swirling grey. It was long-bodied, segmented like an earwig, with dozens of legs tipped in diamond-points that etched white scars into the frozen rock. Its head was a blind bulb of milky chitin, pulsing with a pale, bioluminescent blue that cast long, distorted shadows across the glass.

The toll-keeper, Kaelen thought, his grip tightening on the hilt of his shortsword. He knew the stories. Nothing crossed the Tear without paying the architects, and the architects had long since rotted into peat.

The creature paused ten paces away. Its antennae—thick as willow branches and dripping with freezing condensation—twitching toward Vesper’s pack. Specifically, toward the copper urn strapped to the leather frame. Inside that urn was the pure, rendered fat of a subterranean leviathan, the only fuel hot enough to melt the seals on the Vault of Whispers.

"It wants the tallow," Vesper whispered, her voice dangerously thin.

"It wants us," Kaelen corrected.

He reached behind his back, fingers finding the cold haft of a throwing-axe. The basalt slab beneath his left heel tilted an inch downward. The glass beneath was fracturing now, silver spiderwebs blooming outward from the frost-pocked surface. If he moved too fast, the whole span would shear from the cliff face.

The centipede-thing lunged, its mandibles clicking like dry timber.

Kaelen didn't wait for Vesper to cover him. He dropped his shoulder, slamming his weight against the leaning pylon, and drove the heavy iron axe straight into the creature’s lower joint.

Glass shrieked. The beast reared, a geyser of black, smoking ichor spraying across the translucent bridge, instantly eating through the frost. Vesper didn't hesitate; she swung the heavy copper urn with both hands, smashing the brass rim directly into the creature’s blind, pulsing eye-bulb.

With a sound like breaking church windows, the monster hissed, its numerous legs clawing frantically at the air before its bulk tipped backward. It slipped off the narrow spine, plunging into the grey eternity below, its blue light fading rapidly into the murk.

Silence rushed back, heavier than before.

Kaelen exhaled, a long plume of gray smoke vanishing into the draft. He looked down between his boots. The slab he stood on was no longer attached to the anchor chain. It hung by a single thread of shimmering blue sinew, swinging gently over the abyss.

"Vesper?" he said.

"Move," she rasped, already scrambling across the remaining spans toward the solid black stone of the northern gate. "Just don't look down."

4.title: Decay of the Outer Ring
4.html:
Gravity didn't fail all at once; it stuttered. One second, Sula's mug hovered at chin-height; the next, ceramic shards and black sludge mapped a violent constellation across the scuffed deck plates.

"Hull stress at ninety-four percent," the bulkhead hissed, its synthesized voice clipped and breathless. "Warning: Atmospheric integrity compromised in Sector Seven."

Sula didn't look up from her soldering iron. The blue arc of plasma illuminated the deep lines carved around her eyes, casting frantic shadows against the curved steel wall. She pressed the glowing tip against a hairline fracture in the primary coolant conduit. Hissing steam bit at the air, smelling fiercely of ozone and boiled copper. Her left glove was scorched black across the knuckles, deadened to heat and pain hours ago.

"Sector Seven can bleed," she muttered, her voice raspy from recycling air that tasted of dry dust and old sweat. "Just hold together for twenty more minutes."

Outside the reinforced viewport, the scarred expanse of the Jovian moon hung like a bruised eye, indifferent and massive. Beyond it, the void stretched forever, punctuated by the cold, unblinking glare of distant stars. The orbital station—a rusted wheel of discarded modules and patched-together habitats—creaked in protest as it plunged deeper into the upper fringes of the gas giant's atmosphere. The drag was a physical weight now, a heavy hand pressing against Sula's spine, urging her down.

The red emergency strobes painted the workshop in rhythmic, bleeding gasps. Thump. Thump. Thump. The heartbeat of a dying machine.

A muffled clang echoed through the deck plating, followed by the rapid, uneven slap of magnetic boots. Kael burst through the hatchway, his pressure suit hanging open at the waist, helmet tucked tightly under one arm. His face was slick with grease and sweat, eyes wild in the crimson light.

"The cargo bay is gone," Kael shouted over the shrieking sirens. "Torn clean off by the shear forces. We lost the reserve thrusters."

"I know," Sula said evenly, not breaking her rhythm. She fused the final millimeter of the conduit. The sputtering hiss died, replaced by the steady, high-pitched whine of coolant finally flowing through the repaired line. She lowered the iron, exhaling a long, shuddering breath that cleared the fog from her immediate vision.

Kael grabbed her shoulder, his fingers digging hard through the synthetic fabric of her jacket. "We need to get to the escape pods, Sula. Now. The orbit is decaying too fast. Manual correction won't work."

"There are no pods, Kael. We used the last operational one to launch the core data banks three hours ago." She turned her head, meeting his frantic gaze with eyes that held the flat, heavy stillness of deep water.

Kael froze. The frantic energy drained from his posture, leaving him looking suddenly small inside the oversized frame of his suit. He stared at the glowing blue status light on the conduit, then back to Sula.

"Why?" he whispered.

"Because the data matters. We don't," she replied softly. She reached down, picking up a heavy wrench, and tossed it gently toward him. He caught it by reflex.

"What am I supposed to do with this?"

"Help me seal the inner hatch," Sula said, turning back to the glowing expanse of the viewport. The horizon was no longer black; it was curving sharply, glowing a fierce, terrifying amber as friction ate away at the station's outer skirts. "If we're going to burn, we might as well keep the air inside until the very last second."

Kael looked from the wrench to the window, watching the edge of the world catch fire. Slowly, deliberately, the panic receded from his face, replaced by a grim, quiet resolve. He stepped forward, matching her pace, and jammed the heavy iron dogging bar into the locking mechanism of the door.

Together, they pulled.

5.title: The Taste of Iron
5.html:
The grease on the toggle switch had gone cold and tacky, like congealed lard. Arthur jammed his thumb down anyway. The auxiliary generator gave a wet, pneumatic cough, spat a gout of gray smoke across the concrete floor, and died.

Darkness rushed in, absolute and heavy, smelling of damp limestone and the distinct, coppery tang of a fresh nosebleed. He didn’t reach for his torch. The batteries were dead. They had been dead since Tuesday, when the clicking inside the casing had finally stopped.

Scritch.

It was closer now. Not the cautious, exploratory ticks of the house beetles that lived in the rotting timbers of the adit, but something rhythmic. Intentional. Like a thumbnail dragged slowly across the teeth of a dry comb.

Arthur pressed his back against the damp ribs of the tunnel. His shoulder blades found the smooth, greasy swell of the timber brace. He hadn't built that brace. He’d lived down here forty years, ever since the strike of '84, and he knew every stanchion, every lag screw, every vein of dead quartz in the South Drift. That timber was new. The wood was pale, yellow-white, weeping thick globules of sap that smelled faintly of vinegar.

Scritch. Pause. Scritch-scritch.

He opened his mouth to wet his lips, but his tongue felt like a dry salt-tablet. His fingers found the leather pouch hanging from his belt—the emergency rations. Six lumps of dry salt pork and a sliver of candle. He didn't want the candle. To light it was to admit there was something worth looking at.

Something bumped against his shin.

It was soft, yielding, and cold. Not stone. Not timber.

Arthur froze, his breath locked in his chest, burning the lining of his ribs. He looked down, though he knew the blackness was too thick to offer shape. Whatever was touching his boot leg was damp. It soaked through the heavy wool of his trousers, slick and heavy.
